name.text: NEETUG_BIOLOGY_CH18_SEQUENCING_Q01 - Conduction pathway of cardiac action potential

questiontext.text:
Arrange the following components of the human heart's nodal conducting system in the correct chronological order in which an action potential travels during a heartbeat:

  1. Atrio-ventricular node (AVN)
  2. Sino-atrial node (SAN)
  3. Purkinje fibres
  4. Atrio-ventricular bundle (AV bundle)

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
The human heart is myogenic and contains specialised autoexcitable nodal tissue that initiates and conducts electrical impulses sequentially from the atria to the ventricles.

Step 2: Step-by-Step Sequence
The action potential is first generated by the sino-atrial node (SAN) located in the right upper corner of the right atrium, which acts as the pacemaker, corresponding to (ii). From the SAN, the impulse stimulates atrial contraction and is conducted to the atrio-ventricular node (AVN) at the lower left corner of the right atrium, corresponding to (i). Next, the impulse passes through the atrio-ventricular bundle (AV bundle) emerging on top of the inter-ventricular septum, corresponding to (iv). Finally, the bundle branches give rise to minute Purkinje fibres that transmit the impulse throughout the ventricular musculature, corresponding to (iii).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The correct chronological sequence of conduction is (ii) \(\rightarrow\) (i) \(\rightarrow\) (iv) \(\rightarrow\) (iii).

name.text: NEETUG_BIOLOGY_CH18_SEQUENCING_Q02 - Cascade mechanism of blood coagulation

questiontext.text:
Arrange the following events of blood coagulation in the correct chronological sequence following an injury or trauma:

  1. Conversion of inactive fibrinogen into fibrin threads by thrombin
  2. Formation of the thrombokinase enzyme complex via linked enzymatic reactions
  3. Stimulation of platelets and injured tissues to release clotting-initiating factors
  4. Conversion of inactive prothrombin into active thrombin

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Blood coagulation is a cascade process involving sequential activation of inactive plasma clotting factors in the presence of calcium ions to form a stable fibrin clot.

Step 2: Step-by-Step Sequence
First, an injury or trauma stimulates platelets in the blood and tissues at the injury site to release factors that initiate coagulation, corresponding to (iii). These factors trigger a series of linked enzymatic reactions (cascade process) that form the enzyme complex thrombokinase, corresponding to (ii). Thrombokinase then converts inactive prothrombin present in plasma into active thrombin, corresponding to (iv). Finally, thrombin converts inactive plasma fibrinogen into insoluble fibrin threads that trap dead and damaged formed elements to form a clot, corresponding to (i).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The correct chronological sequence of blood coagulation is (iii) \(\rightarrow\) (ii) \(\rightarrow\) (iv) \(\rightarrow\) (i).

name.text: NEETUG_BIOLOGY_CH18_SEQUENCING_Q03 - Sequential events of the human cardiac cycle

questiontext.text:
Starting from atrial contraction, arrange the following events of a single cardiac cycle in the correct chronological sequence:

  1. Atrial systole increases the flow of blood into the ventricles by about 30 per cent
  2. Ventricular diastole causes ventricular pressure to fall, resulting in closure of the semilunar valves
  3. Ventricular systole closes the tricuspid and bicuspid valves and forces open the semilunar valves
  4. Further decline in ventricular pressure allows atrial pressure to push open the tricuspid and bicuspid valves, returning the heart to joint diastole

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
The cardiac cycle consists of cyclically repeated systole and diastole of both the atria and ventricles, driven by action potentials from the SAN and resulting pressure gradients across heart valves.

Step 2: Step-by-Step Sequence
Beginning at atrial contraction, the SAN generates an action potential causing simultaneous atrial systole, which increases blood flow into the ventricles by about 30 per cent, corresponding to (i). The impulse is then conducted to the ventricles, causing ventricular systole; rising ventricular pressure closes the tricuspid and bicuspid valves and forces open the semilunar valves to eject blood into the pulmonary artery and aorta, corresponding to (iii). Next, the ventricles relax (ventricular diastole) and ventricular pressure falls, causing the semilunar valves to close to prevent backflow into the ventricles, corresponding to (ii). As ventricular pressure declines further, blood in the atria pushes open the tricuspid and bicuspid valves, allowing free flow into the ventricles and returning all four chambers to joint diastole, corresponding to (iv).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The correct chronological sequence of events is (i) \(\rightarrow\) (iii) \(\rightarrow\) (ii) \(\rightarrow\) (iv).
